title: Why the origin of evil is hard to know
source_text: Μετὰ ταῦτά φησιν ὁ Κέλσος· τίς ἡ τῶν κακῶν γένεσις, οὐ ῥᾴδιον μὲν γνῶναι τῷ μὴ φιλοσοφήσαντι, ἐξαρκεῖ δ᾿ εἰς πλῆθος εἰρῆσθαι ὡς ἐκ θεοῦ μὲν οὐκ ἔστι κακὰ, ὕλῃ δὲ πρόσκειται καὶ τοῖς θνητοῖς ἐμπολιτεύεται· ὁμοία δ᾿ ἀπ᾿ ἀρχῆς εἰς τέλος ἡ τῶν θνητῶν περίοδος, καὶ κατὰ τὰς τεταγμένας ἀνακυκλήσεις ἀνάγκη τὰ αὐτὰ ἀεὶ καὶ γεγονέναι καὶ εἶναι καὶ ἔσεσθαι. καὶ ὁ μὲν Κέλσος φησὶ τὴν τῶν κακῶν γένεσιν οὐ ῥᾴδιον εἶναι γνῶναι τῷ μὴ φιλοσοφήσαντι, ὡς τοῦ μὲν φιλοσοφοῦντος γνῶναι τὴν γένεσιν αὐτῶν δυναμένου ῥᾳδίως, τοῦ δὲ μὴ φιλοσοφοῦντος οὐ ῥᾳδίως μὲν οἵου τε ὄντος θεωρεῖν τὴν γένεσιν τῶν κακῶν, πλὴν εἰ καὶ μετὰ καμάτου ἀλλά γε δυνατοῦ ὄντος γνῶναι. ἡμεῖς δὲ καὶ πρὸς τοῦτό φαμεν ὅτι τὴν τῶν κακῶν γένεσιν οὐδὲ τῷ φιλοσοφήσαντι γνῶναι ῥᾴδιον, τάχα δὲ οὐδὲ τούτοις καθαρῶς αὐτὴν γνῶναι δυνατὸν, ἐὰν μὴ θεοῦ ἐπιπνοίᾳ καὶ τίνα τὰ κακὰ τρανωθῇ καὶ πῶς ὑπέστη δηλωθῇ καὶ τίνα τρόπον ἀφανισθήσεται νοηθῇ. ἐν κακοῖς γοῦν οὔσης καὶ τῆς περὶ θεοῦ ἀγνοίας, ὄντος δὲ μεγίστου κακοῦ καὶ τοῦ μὴ εἰδέναι τὸν τρόπον τῆς τοῦ θεοῦ θεραπείας καὶ τῆς εἰς αὐτὸν εὐσεβείας, πάντως μὲν καὶ κατὰ Κέλσον τινὲς τῶν φιλοσοφησάντων οὐκ ἔγνωσαν, ὅπερ δῆλόν ἐστιν ἐκ τῶν διαφόρων ἐν φιλοσοφίᾳ αἱρέσεων· καθ᾿ ἡμᾶς δὲ οὐδεὶς μὴ ἐγνωκὼς κακὸν εἶναι τὸ νομίζειν εὐσέβειαν σῴζεσθαι ἐν τοῖς καθεστηκόσι κατὰ τὰς κοινότερον νοουμένας πολιτείας νόμοις οἷός τε ἔσται τὴν γένεσιν γνῶναι τῶν κακῶν. καὶ οὐδεὶς μὴ διαλαβὼν τὰ περὶ τοῦ καλουμένου διαβόλου καὶ τῶν ἀγγέλων αὐτοῦ, τίς τε πρὸ τοῦ διάβολος γεγενῆσθαι οὗτος ἦν καὶ πῶς γεγένηται διάβολος καὶ τίς ἡ αἰτία τοῦ συναποστῆναι αὐτῷ τοὺς καλουμένους αὐτοῦ ἀγγέλους, οἷός τε ἔσται γνῶναι τὴν γένεσιν τῶν κακῶν. δεῖ δὲ τὸν μέλλοντα ταύτην εἰδέναι καὶ περὶ δαιμόνων ἀκριβέστερον διειληφέναι ὅτι τε μή εἰσι, καθὸ δαίμονές εἰσι, δημιουργήματα τοῦ θεοῦ, ἀλλὰ μόνον καθὸ λογικοί τινες, καὶ πόθεν ἐληλύθασιν ἐπὶ τὸ τοιοῦτοι γενέσθαι, ὡς ἐν καταστάσει δαιμόνων αὐτῶν ὑποστῆναι τὸ ἡγεμονικόν. εἴπερ οὖν ἄλλος τις τόπος τῶν ἐν ἀνθρώποις ἐξετάσεως δεόμενος δυσθήρατός ἐστι τῇ φύσει ἡμῶν, ἐν τούτοις καὶ ἡ τῶν κακῶν ταχθείη ἂν γένεσις.
pass_a_gloss: After these Celsus says: 'what the coming-to-be (γένεσις) of evils [is], is not easy (ῥᾴδιον) to know for one who has not philosophised (μὴ φιλοσοφήσαντι), but it suffices (ἐξαρκεῖ) to have been said to the multitude (εἰς πλῆθος) that evils are not from God, but adhere (πρόσκειται) to matter and dwell as citizens (ἐμπολιτεύεται) among mortals (θνητοῖς); and alike (ὁμοία) from beginning to end [is] the cycle (περίοδος) of mortals, and according to the ordered (τεταγμένας) revolutions (ἀνακυκλήσεις) it is necessary (ἀνάγκη) that the same things always have been and be and will be'. And Celsus says the coming-to-be of evils is not easy to know for one not having philosophised, as the one philosophising being able easily to know their coming-to-be, but the one not philosophising not being easily able to see (θεωρεῖν) the coming-to-be of evils, yet, even if with toil (καμάτου), being able to know. But we say also to this that the coming-to-be of evils is not easy to know even for one having philosophised, and perhaps not even for these is it possible to know it purely (καθαρῶς), unless by inspiration (ἐπιπνοίᾳ) of God both what the evils are be made clear (τρανωθῇ) and how they came to subsist (ὑπέστη) be shown and in what manner they will be made to vanish (ἀφανισθήσεται) be understood (νοηθῇ). Ignorance (ἀγνοίας) about God then being among evils, and the greatest (μεγίστου) evil being also not to know the manner of the service (θεραπείας) of God and of piety (εὐσεβείας) toward him, certainly also according to Celsus some of the philosophisers did not know, which is clear from the different sects (αἱρέσεων) in philosophy; but according to us no one not having known (ἐγνωκώς) [that] it is evil to think piety is preserved (σῴζεσθαι) in the laws established according to the more commonly understood polities (πολιτείας) will be able to know the coming-to-be of evils. And no one not having grasped (διαλαβών) the things about the so-called devil (διαβόλου) and his angels (ἀγγέλων), both who this one was before becoming devil and how he became devil and what the cause (αἰτία) of his so-called angels revolting with (συναποστῆναι) him, will be able to know the coming-to-be of evils. But the one about to know this must also have distinguished more precisely about demons (δαιμόνων), both that they are not, insofar as (καθό) they are demons, creations (δημιουργήματα) of God, but only insofar as [they are] some rational (λογικοί) [beings], and whence they came to become such, so that their ruling part (ἡγεμονικόν) came to subsist in the state (καταστάσει) of demons. If then any other topic (τόπος) of things among men needing examination is hard to hunt down (δυσθήρατος) for our nature, among these also the coming-to-be of evils would be ranked (ταχθείη).
pass_b_english: After this Celsus says: “What the origin of evils is, is not easy to know for one who has not studied philosophy. But it is enough to say to the multitude that evils are not from God, but cling to matter and have their home among mortals. The cycle of mortal things is alike from beginning to end, and by the appointed revolutions it must be that the same things always have been, are, and will be.”

Celsus says that the origin of evils is not easy to know for one who has not studied philosophy. He speaks as though the man who studies philosophy could know their origin easily, while the man who does not cannot easily see the origin of evils, yet can know it, even if only with toil. But to this too we say that the origin of evils is not easy to know even for one who has studied philosophy. Perhaps it is not possible even for such men to know it clearly, unless by the inspiration of God it is made plain what evils are, and shown how they came to exist, and understood in what way they will be done away with.

At any rate, ignorance about God is itself among evils, and the greatest evil is not to know the way to serve God and to show Him reverence. Certainly, even according to Celsus, some of those who studied philosophy did not know this, as is plain from the different schools in philosophy. But according to us, no one will be able to know the origin of evils who has not recognised that it is an evil to think that reverence for God is kept safe in the laws established in states as they are commonly understood.

Nor will anyone be able to know the origin of evils who has not grasped what concerns the one called the devil and his angels (Matthew 25:41): who this one was before he became the devil, how he became the devil, and what caused those called his angels to fall away with him. Whoever is to know this origin must also have understood more precisely about demons: that they are not God’s handiwork in so far as they are demons, but only in so far as they are rational beings of some kind; and from what cause they have come to be such that their ruling part came to exist in the condition of demons. If, then, any other subject among human questions needing examination is hard for our nature to track down, the origin of evils may be counted among these.

choices.choice: Celsus's last clause: stiff 'must always have been, be, and be going to be' -> 'it must be that the same things always have been, are, and will be'
γοῦν: 'certainly' -> 'At any rate' (avoids two 'certainly's and keeps the particle); καί rendered 'itself among evils'
inspiration clause: three parallel passives tidied ('made plain ... and shown ... and understood')
Matthew 25:41 checked ('the devil and his angels')

'The devil and his angels' is a clear allusion to Matthew 25:41 ('the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels'); cited inline. The falling away of his angels with him may also recall Revelation 12:7-9, but Origen quotes no words from it, so it is left uncited. Celsus's word ἐμπολιτεύεται ('dwell as citizens among') is rendered 'have their home among'; πρόσκειται 'cling to'. εὐσέβεια is rendered 'reverence for God' / 'show Him reverence' rather than 'piety' for readability; θεραπεία 'serve'. 'Itself among evils' renders the καί of καὶ τῆς περὶ θεοῦ ἀγνοίας. 'States as they are commonly understood' renders κατὰ τὰς κοινότερον νοουμένας πολιτείας: ordinary earthly cities, as against the heavenly commonwealth. γένεσις is rendered 'origin' throughout, following Celsus's question. Celsus's final clause on cycles is answered in 4.67.
